findings.issue_text: canManage() treats the global view scope as manage permission, allowing all-groups view-only admins to create groups via requireManage()-guarded endpoints

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns authorization resource IDs instead of Keycloak group IDs/resource names, causing individual-group view-members/manage-members grants to fail user filtering and counts
Removing usersEvaluator::canView makes an empty group-ID set disable user filtering, exposing users to callers with query-users but no user-view or group-member permission

goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Removing usersEvaluator::canView makes an empty group-ID set disable user filtering, exposing users to callers with query-users but no user-view or group-member permission

adjudication.rationale: The finding misreads the code. Looking at the diff in UsersResource.java, the searchForUser method now sets session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds) when groupIds is not empty. When groupIds IS empty (meaning user has no group-level view permissions), the attribute is simply not set. The user search is then performed by session.users().searchForUserStream() which will use this attribute to filter results. The key insight is that getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns empty set when root.users().canView() is true (meaning user has full view access), so the filtering logic is: if user can view all users, no group filtering needed; if user has specific group permissions, filter by those groups. The removal of the .filter(usersEvaluator::canView) is intentional because the filtering is now handled at the query level via the session attribute. This is not a bug - it's a refactoring of how permissions are applied.
